title: RHCSA preparation • System administration on RHEL 10
description: Study RHEL 10 administration on Windows, macOS or Linux with two local virtual machines, ten graded labs, two rehearsals and a reboot-verified final practical.

modules.title: Start here • Working with the two machines
Shell scripts that other users can run

lessons.title: Set up your workspace and take a baseline
lessons.body:
You are the on-call administrator for a small office. The server supplies files and services. The client represents the workstation whose users need them. By the final practical you will make changes on both machines, verify them from the affected user's point of view, and leave them working after startup.

## Before you begin
You should be comfortable typing basic shell commands and using a text editor. The reading and quizzes work in Erudior. The desktop app runs a client and server on your computer. Windows uses Debian under WSL 2, macOS uses a local Lima instance named `erudior-labs`, and Linux uses QEMU directly. Open **First-time setup** in a VM lesson for your platform's instructions. Inside the Linux provider, install QEMU 9.2 or newer and a prepared, BIOS-bootable x86-64 RHEL 10 or compatible cloud image. The host supplies both guests from the same image. Reserve 3 GiB for the two guests, plus memory for the provider and the desktop.

For Red Hat package parity, use an entitled RHEL 10 image. The engine supplies cloud-init configuration and a learner account. The local image must already contain the RHCSA services and tools listed in the engine's **docs/VM_LABS.md**. Place it inside the provider at `~/.local/share/erudior-vm-labs/images/linux-nfs-autofs-v1.qcow2` for the default data directory.

## Make a baseline
Open **Practice consoles and an on-demand mount**, select **Start lab**, and wait for both guests. Open each console in turn. Under **Console login** find this attempt's credentials for `learner`. Run the following in each guest.

```sh
hostname
cat /etc/redhat-release
id
ip -brief address
cat /proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id
```

Write down which guest owns `192.168.77.10` and which owns `192.168.77.20`. Hostname, address and boot ID together identify where and when you observed an outcome. If the prompt is silent during first boot, let cloud-init finish and press Enter. Use `sudo` for changes inside these guests. If the learner or guest address differs, confirm you opened a console from this lesson.

## How to study
Use the untimed pair for the worked examples. Return to the same lesson to resume it. A graded lesson opens its own fresh pair on the first attempt. **Prepare machines** boots the pair and **Begin** starts the deadline. In a timed attempt, leaving the lesson keeps the clock running. When switching lessons, stop the untimed workspace with **Stop lab**, or stop a completed practical after its result is saved. This keeps just two guests running on the host. Stopping the pair preserves its disks. **Reset disks** discards that lesson's guest changes. The final samples ten tasks. Do the self-checks as well to practice the wider EX200 objectives.

lessons.title: Practice consoles and an on-demand mount
lessons.body:
This is your reusable workshop. You can open both consoles here while following later lessons. **Check my work** in this workspace grades only the on-demand network mount. You can return after the file systems module and repeat the check.

## Trace a request between the guests
On the server, run `sudo exportfs -v` and `cat /srv/projects/erudior-lab.txt`. Note the allowed client and the first few characters of the file. On the client, run `ip route get 192.168.77.10`. Look for the outgoing interface and source address. Confirm both guests' addresses before editing.

## Make one mount work
On the client, create `/etc/auto.master.d/workshop.autofs` containing the first line below. Create `/etc/auto.workshop` containing the second line. Each file has one line. A direct map uses a full client path as its key.

```text
/- /etc/auto.workshop
/mnt/projects -fstype=nfs,ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects
```

Run `sudo systemctl enable --now autofs` and `sudo systemctl reload autofs`. Then run `cat /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` and `findmnt -T /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` on the client. Expect the same marker as on the server and an NFS filesystem. A missing path calls for checking the master file's `.autofs` suffix, the map key and the service journal.

Choose **Check my work** when ready. It reboots the client and checks again. Read the before/after observations. Reopen this lesson for future walkthroughs and keep your own evidence in a notebook. In later graded labs, keep working until you have checked the requested state, then choose **Submit exam**.

lessons.title: Find evidence and build a shared directory
lessons.body:
A colleague reports that overnight copies failed. Work as learner on the untimed client. Make a private practice directory and turn a noisy log into an archive someone else can inspect.

```sh
mkdir -p ~/rhcsa-tools && cd ~/rhcsa-tools
printf '%s\n' 'OK copied' 'ERR read' 'OK copied' 'ERR write' > run.log
grep '^ERR ' run.log | sort > errors.txt
wc -l < errors.txt
ln run.log run.hard
ln -s run.log run.link
ls -li run*
tar -czf evidence.tar.gz run.log errors.txt
tar -tzf evidence.tar.gz
```

Expect two errors, the same inode for the two hard-linked names, and a symbolic link containing a pathname. Rename `run.log` to `night.log`. Predict which link still reads the log, then test each. Capture the failed read with `cat run.link 2>link-error.txt`. Restore the name and verify the symbolic link works again. Create a bzip2 version with `tar -cjf evidence.tar.bz2 run.log` after restoring the name. Extract an archive into a new empty directory with `tar -xf evidence.tar.gz -C unpacked` after creating `unpacked` with `mkdir unpacked`. Compare the recovered file with `cmp`. Look up flags using `man tar`, `info coreutils` or `/usr/share/doc`.

## A directory shared by a team
On the server, create a practice group with `sudo groupadd editors` if absent. Run `sudo install -d -g editors -m 2770 /srv/editorial`. With `stat -c '%A %a %G' /srv/editorial` expect `drwxrws--- 2770 editors`. Directory execute permission allows traversal. Setgid makes newly created children inherit the directory's group. It does not grant write permission by itself.

Try it with `sudo touch /srv/editorial/draft` and inspect the group on the child. If a user cannot enter a path despite suitable final permissions, inspect every ancestor with `namei -l /srv/editorial/draft`. In a clean practice directory, try `cp`, `mv`, a text editor, and `rm -i` on your own disposable file to practice the file lifecycle.

lessons.title: Lab • Hand off a team workspace
lessons.body:
On the **server**, prepare `/srv/team` for `labops`. This group is local to the server. Create it here if needed. Team members need full directory access, others need none, and new entries should inherit the team group. The requested final mode is `2770`.

Before submission, inspect the directory itself, create a disposable child inside it, and check the child's group. Remove your test child. If the mode reads `0770`, identify which special bit is missing. If the group is wrong only on a child created earlier, repeat with a new file. Submit when the directory is correct and review the post-reboot result.

lessons.title: Onboard an operator without losing existing access
lessons.body:
An operator should join a second team without losing an earlier assignment. On the untimed client, use spare names for this exercise. Check `getent passwd fieldops` and `getent group dispatch` first. On a fresh guest the names should be unused.

```sh
sudo groupadd dispatch
sudo groupadd editors-local
sudo useradd -m -G dispatch fieldops
sudo usermod -aG editors-local fieldops
id fieldops
sudo chage -M 90 -W 7 fieldops
sudo chage -l fieldops
sudo -iu fieldops id
```

Expect both supplementary groups and a 90-day maximum age. `usermod -G` replaces the supplementary list unless you append. Existing shells keep their group credentials until a new login. Set a password interactively with `sudo passwd fieldops` and verify the aging policy again. Avoid putting passwords in shell history.

## Delegate one administrative action
Locate `systemctl` with `command -v systemctl`. Use `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/fieldops-status` to grant the exact command (adjust its path if necessary).

```text
fieldops ALL=(root) /usr/bin/systemctl is-active chronyd.service
```

Run `sudo visudo -c` and `sudo -l -U fieldops`. Compare the granted command and arguments to the request. To retire only this practice identity, remove the new sudoers entry, run `sudo userdel -r fieldops`, then remove only the two groups you created after checking their membership. Verify the lookups now return no record. A local account or group on the client has a separate database from one with the same name on the server.

lessons.title: Lab • Add a client operator
lessons.body:
On the **client**, create the local account `labtech` and give it membership in `labops`. Preserve any other membership the account has. The group on the server belongs to the other guest and cannot grant access here.

Check `getent passwd labtech`, `getent group labops` and `id labtech`. A blank member list in a group record can still be consistent with a primary group, so judge effective membership with `id`. Switch to a fresh login context to see the groups a new process would receive. Submit and compare the membership checks across the reboot.

lessons.title: Choose and verify a software source
lessons.body:
A branch office receives software over removable media. DNF needs a repository root containing `repodata/repomd.xml`. The URL refers to that root. A repository ID identifies the entry to DNF, while `name` is a human-readable label.

## Inspect a local repository
The client includes an empty practice repository. In the untimed client create `/etc/yum.repos.d/workshop.repo` with this content, then validate only that source.

```ini
[workshop]
name=Workshop shelf
baseurl=file:///srv/erudior-repo
enabled=1
gpgcheck=1
```

```sh
test -r /srv/erudior-repo/repodata/repomd.xml
dnf repolist --enabled
sudo dnf --disablerepo='*' --enablerepo=workshop makecache
rpm -q bash
rpm -qf /usr/bin/bash
```

Metadata refresh should succeed even though this shelf has no application packages. Package signature checking applies to actual RPM transactions. In a RHEL guest with a trusted RPM and its dependencies staged, run `rpmkeys --checksig ./package.rpm` on the real file, install with `sudo dnf install ./package.rpm`, then verify with `rpm -q NAME`. On an entitled guest use `dnf repolist` to identify the enabled Red Hat sources and `sudo dnf upgrade NAME` to update a chosen practice package. Review the transaction before removing the practice package with `sudo dnf remove NAME`. Substitute the actual package name throughout.

## Self-check with a Flatpak remote
Use a guest with Flatpak, a reachable authorized remote descriptor and a practice application. Run `flatpak remote-add --user --if-not-exists training /path/to/training.flatpakrepo` using the supplied real descriptor. List `flatpak remote-ls --user --app training`, choose a listed application ID, run `flatpak install --user training APP_ID`, and verify it appears in `flatpak list --user --app`. Remove the same app with `flatpak uninstall --user APP_ID` and verify it disappears. A user installation and a system-wide installation have different scopes. These package transactions require additional software media or a reachable source.

lessons.title: Lab • Bring an offline RPM source online
lessons.body:
On the **client**, enable one DNF repository named `erudior-local` using only `file:///srv/erudior-repo` as its base URL and require RPM signature checks. The files under that directory are supplied. Complete the task with the prepared local content.

Verify that the enabled repository list shows the ID, that a metadata refresh restricted to that ID succeeds, and that its configuration sets `gpgcheck=1`. Watch for an extra `repodata` component, a duplicate section ID in another file, or a stale `mirrorlist` or `metalink`. The supplied shelf is empty, so an empty list of available packages can accompany a working configuration.

lessons.title: Turn a shell command into a testable tool
lessons.body:
The next shift needs a tool that can report on several files without losing a filename that contains spaces. A script has a contract. Specify its arguments, output, exit status and required permissions before you write it.

In your home directory, save this as `line-report`. The first line selects the interpreter when the file is executed directly. Quotes around `"$@"` preserve the original arguments individually.

```sh
#!/bin/sh
if [ "$#" -eq 0 ]; then
    printf '%s\n' 'supply at least one file' >&2
    exit 2
fi
for file in "$@"; do
    if [ -f "$file" ] && [ -r "$file" ]; then
        lines=$(wc -l < "$file")
        printf '%s %s\n' "$lines" "$file"
    else
        printf 'unreadable: %s\n' "$file" >&2
        exit 1
    fi
done
```

Run `chmod 755 line-report`. Create a file containing two newline-terminated lines named `shift notes`. Run `./line-report 'shift notes'` and check for `2 shift notes`. Run `./line-report missing >out.txt 2>err.txt`, immediately check `echo $?`, and inspect both files. An error belongs on standard error so the next program can use standard output as data.

## Try a numeric boundary
Make a second executable that reads its first argument as a number and prints `low` below 5 and `high` otherwise. Use the shell numeric test `[ "$1" -lt 5 ]`, leaving spaces around the bracket tokens. Exercise 0, 4, 5 and 17. Try launching the installed script by its full path as a second user. A script that works only when invoked with `bash scriptname` may have a bad shebang or lack execute permission.

lessons.title: Lab • Deliver an executable classifier
lessons.body:
On the **client**, install `/usr/local/bin/lab-classify` as an executable shell script for an unprivileged user. Given one nonnegative integer, it must print exactly `small` below 10 and `large` for 10 or higher. The command should run directly by absolute path.

Write your own tests first. Include 0, 9, 10 and a larger value you choose. Run them as `learner` and compare the exact standard output. If a root-run test works and a learner test fails, inspect the shebang, directory traversal and file mode. Extra prompts or debug output on stdout change the result.

lessons.title: Follow a slowdown from process to journal
lessons.body:
A server is sluggish after a scheduled job. Start with evidence from the current boot. On the workshop server, run `uptime`, `free -h` and `ps -eo pid,user,ni,pcpu,pmem,comm --sort=-pcpu | head`. Reorder by `-pmem` to find memory consumers. Load, CPU use and memory pressure answer different questions.

## Follow one process you own
```sh
nice -n 5 sleep 300 &
jobpid=$!
ps -o pid,ni,stat,comm -p "$jobpid"
renice -n 10 -p "$jobpid"
kill -TERM "$jobpid"
wait "$jobpid"
```

Expect the nice value to rise from 5 to 10 and the process to exit after TERM. A higher nice number gives a normal process a lower scheduling priority. Diagnose a service with `systemctl status NAME` and `journalctl -b -u NAME`, replacing NAME with the unit. Record the first failure and its timestamp. To preserve messages on a default journald setup using `Storage=auto`, create `/var/log/journal` with sudo, run `sudo systemd-tmpfiles --create --prefix /var/log/journal` then `sudo journalctl --flush`. If policy explicitly sets volatile storage, configure `Storage=persistent` in a journald drop-in and restart journald. Write `logger 'workshop boot evidence'`. After a planned workshop reboot check `journalctl -b -1 -t "$USER"` or search the previous boot by message.

## Choose a tuning profile
Run `tuned-adm list`, `tuned-adm recommend` and `tuned-adm active`. Record the current profile name before changing it. On the workshop server choose an installed profile such as `balanced` with `sudo tuned-adm profile balanced`. Verify with `tuned-adm active` and `sudo tuned-adm verify`. Explain why maximizing throughput and reducing energy use can favor different settings. Restore the prior profile when finished.

lessons.title: Practice a one-time boot change and restore normal startup
lessons.body:
In the untimed server, run `systemctl get-default`, `systemctl list-units --type=target --state=active` and `cat /proc/cmdline`. The configured default is the goal for a normal startup. The running boot can have reached several targets at once.

## Self-check at a local VM console
Use a disposable RHEL 10 guest with a visible bootloader console and known authorized administrative credentials for rescue mode. Some cloud images lock the root account or hide the early boot menu. Use a suitable console-equipped practice image for this exercise. Keep the graded pair's boot options intact.

At the GRUB menu highlight the current kernel, press `e`, append `systemd.unit=rescue.target` to the kernel command line, and use the on-screen boot key (usually Ctrl+x). Authenticate when prompted. Run `cat /proc/cmdline` and `systemctl is-active rescue.target`. Resume normal service with `systemctl default`. Reboot normally and confirm the one-time kernel argument has disappeared. For a headless server, practice configuring `multi-user.target` as the default with `sudo systemctl set-default multi-user.target`. Verify with `systemctl get-default`. Restore the original default when finished.

On a RHEL guest with `grubby`, inspect `sudo grubby --info=DEFAULT`. Practice a reversible persistent change to the default kernel entry: save its path using `kernel=$(grubby --default-kernel)`, add an informational argument with `sudo grubby --update-kernel="$kernel" --args="systemd.show_status=yes"`, then inspect the entry. After booting that entry, check `/proc/cmdline`. Remove only your added argument with `sudo grubby --update-kernel="$kernel" --remove-args="systemd.show_status=yes"`, reselecting the saved path if you logged in anew. Start and stop guests cleanly with `systemctl reboot` and `systemctl poweroff` in a disposable console exercise.

lessons.title: Lab • Apply a persistent performance profile
lessons.body:
On the **server**, select the provided TuneD `throughput-performance` profile. The server must report that profile after startup without an interactive command.

Inspect the service state, the installed profiles and the chosen profile independently. If the name is present in the profile list but the active profile differs, determine which command selects it. If the choice vanishes after startup, examine the TuneD service and its current-boot journal. Use the grader's before/after observations to check whether your change survived.

lessons.title: Build and extend a disposable LVM volume
lessons.body:
A department needs a filesystem that can grow without moving its existing data. A partition can hold an LVM physical volume (PV). A volume group (VG) pools capacity. A logical volume (LV) draws space from the pool. Growing the LV and growing the filesystem are distinct operations.

## Self-check using a new file as a practice disk
Use a disposable RHEL guest with loop devices, parted, LVM2 and XFS tools. Run the blocks in the same root shell (`sudo -i`). Use only the newly allocated loop device reported below. Stop if `vgs workshp_vg` already finds a group with that name, or `/mnt/workshp_lv` is already in use. This exercise needs about 1 GiB of free space. The regular-file disk lets you practice without repartitioning a system disk.

```sh
diskfile=$(mktemp /var/tmp/rhcsa-disk.XXXXXX)
truncate -s 1G "$diskfile"
loop=$(losetup --find --show --partscan "$diskfile")
losetup "$loop"
parted -s "$loop" mklabel gpt mkpart primary 1MiB 100%
partprobe "$loop"
udevadm settle
part="$loop"p1
lsblk -o PATH,SIZE,TYPE,FSTYPE "$loop"
```

Confirm the partition path shown by `lsblk` equals `$part`. If the LVM devices file is in use and the partition is not visible to LVM, add only the practice partition with `lvmdevices --adddev "$part"`. An image filtering loop devices may require an attached unused training disk instead. Do not substitute the boot disk.

```sh
pvcreate "$part"
vgcreate workshp_vg "$part"
lvcreate -L 400M -n reports workshp_vg
mkfs.xfs /dev/workshp_vg/reports
mkdir /mnt/workshp_lv
mount /dev/workshp_vg/reports /mnt/workshp_lv
printf 'keep me\n' > /mnt/workshp_lv/proof
df -hT /mnt/workshp_lv
lvextend -L +128M -r /dev/workshp_vg/reports
cat /mnt/workshp_lv/proof
df -hT /mnt/workshp_lv
lvs
```

Expect more space and unchanged proof text. `-r` requests a matching filesystem resize. Use `pvs`, `vgs` and `lvs` to find which layer lacks space if growth fails. A loop mapping lasts only for this exercise. Practice mounting by UUID across reboot on an attached practice disk in the next module.

## Clean up the disk you created
After confirming `losetup "$loop"` still shows your temporary file and `findmnt /mnt/workshp_lv` identifies your practice LV, unmount it. Remove the practice LV, then the VG, then its PV label using `lvremove /dev/workshp_vg/reports`, `vgremove workshp_vg` and `pvremove "$part"`. If you added the partition to the LVM devices file, remove its entry if still present. Delete partition 1 on that loop disk with `parted -s "$loop" rm 1`, detach with `losetup -d "$loop"`, then remove your temporary file and empty mount directory. Check `lvs` and `losetup -j "$diskfile"` to confirm retirement.

lessons.title: Activate swap and make it return at startup
lessons.body:
Swap supplies extra backing space for idle memory pages. An allocated file, a swap signature, activation now and a boot-time entry are four distinct states. On the untimed server inspect `free -h`, `swapon --show --bytes`, `df -h /var/lib` and `findmnt -T /var/lib`. Use the following on the workshop guest's local XFS or ext4 filesystem. Choose a fresh path and ensure at least 70 MiB is free.

```sh
sudo sh -c 'set -C; umask 077; dd if=/dev/zero bs=1M count=65 status=none > /var/lib/workshop.swap'
```

If creation failed or the path already existed, stop and choose a new path. Inspect the resulting regular file and mode with `sudo stat /var/lib/workshop.swap`. Initialize your new file with `sudo mkswap /var/lib/workshop.swap` and activate it with `sudo swapon /var/lib/workshop.swap`. Verify the name and size with `swapon --show --bytes`. Allocating real blocks avoids sparse-file activation errors.

Edit `/etc/fstab` and add one line `/var/lib/workshop.swap none swap defaults 0 0` after confirming that path has no existing entry. Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload` and `sudo findmnt --verify`. Reboot the untimed guest and run `swapon --show` again. A clean configuration file alone cannot prove that the kernel activated the space.

lessons.title: Lab • Add persistent swap capacity
lessons.body:
On the **server**, add an active swap file at `/var/lib/erudior.swap` with at least 64 MiB usable and make it activate automatically at boot. Leave existing swap and filesystem entries intact. A 65 MiB allocation leaves room for the swap header.

Use `swapon --show --bytes` to confirm the path and usable size. Check that the regular file is private to root, its entry appears once in `/etc/fstab`, and the file is fully allocated. If the grader sees the file now but loses it after boot, inspect the boot-time configuration and swap unit journal.

lessons.title: Mount the right filesystem and prove what is serving a path
lessons.body:
On the server inspect `lsblk -f`, `findmnt -T /` and `sudo blkid`. Device names can change after hardware changes. A filesystem UUID or unique label identifies the intended filesystem across boots. A mounted filesystem also hides whatever was in the mount directory underneath it.

## Self-check with disposable filesystems
Use the preceding lesson's new-file and loop procedure on a disposable guest, with a fresh backing file for each filesystem. For each new empty partition, choose **one** formatter: `mkfs.ext4 -L TRAINEXT "$part"`, `mkfs.xfs -L TRAINXFS "$part"`, or `mkfs.vfat -n TRAINVF "$part"`. VFAT needs dosfstools. Never reformat a partition whose data you intend to keep. Create an empty practice mountpoint, mount the partition, write and read a marker, and use `findmnt -T /path/to/marker` to record the source and type. Unmount, verify the marker disappears, remount and verify it returns. VFAT generally expresses ownership and masks through mount options.

For a boot test, use a persistent, attached practice disk. Mount its filesystem by UUID or by LABEL at a new path. For example, with an ext4 volume add a single `UUID=actual-uuid /mnt/reports ext4 defaults 0 2` line to `/etc/fstab`, using the real identifier from `blkid`. Create the mountpoint, unmount any manual mount, reload systemd, run `sudo findmnt --verify` and `sudo mount /mnt/reports`. Verify the source and marker after a reboot. Remove the entry before retiring the disk.

## Self-check the network path
In the untimed client, mount the supplied server export once at a separate empty location. Run `sudo mkdir -p /mnt/nfs-check`, `sudo mount -t nfs -o ro 192.168.77.10:/srv/projects /mnt/nfs-check` and inspect the marker with `findmnt -T /mnt/nfs-check/erudior-lab.txt`. Unmount this test with `sudo umount /mnt/nfs-check`. Compare that manual mount with the direct map from orientation. Autofs installs a trigger; reading a path makes the NFS mount appear. A local directory with a copied file cannot supply the live server's data.

lessons.title: Lab • Recover a share on demand
lessons.body:
On the **client**, configure autofs for the read-only server export `192.168.77.10:/srv/projects` at `/mnt/projects`. The application must be able to open `/mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt` on demand, including after the client restarts.

Start by reading the marker at its source on the server. On the client check the master map include, your direct-map key, and the autofs service state. Trigger the mount by opening the marker. Inspect the exact file with `findmnt -T /mnt/projects/erudior-lab.txt`. If the client can mount the export manually at another empty directory but the application path fails, inspect your autofs maps and `journalctl -b -u autofs`. Submit to check the post-reboot behavior.

lessons.title: Make a service leave evidence on every boot
lessons.body:
A service can be running now and absent after reboot. It can also be enabled and failing on every start. Use a practice oneshot unit to observe what each state means. On the workshop server save the following in `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-stamp.service`.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Record workshop startup

[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/touch /run/workshop-stamp
RemainAfterExit=yes

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload`, then `sudo systemctl start workshop-stamp`. Compare `systemctl is-active workshop-stamp` with `systemctl is-enabled workshop-stamp`. The first should report active and the second disabled on this new unit. Now enable it with `sudo systemctl enable workshop-stamp`. Verify the marker with `stat /run/workshop-stamp`. Because /run is recreated at startup, seeing this marker after reboot is good evidence of a new service invocation.

Self-check: stop the practice unit and predict both state queries before running them. Start it again and inspect `systemctl cat workshop-stamp` and `journalctl -b -u workshop-stamp`. Distinguish the installed definition, systemd's loaded view and the program's actual outcome. A successful oneshot with RemainAfterExit can legitimately show `active (exited)`.

lessons.title: Choose a scheduler and verify its work
lessons.body:
Schedule a job that records a harmless timestamp. In an untimed guest with `at` and `atd` installed and active, run `echo '/usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-once.log' | at now + 2 minutes`. Use `atq` while waiting. The job leaves the queue after execution; check the actual log. For recurring work in an image with cronie and active crond, use `crontab -e` and add `*/2 * * * * /usr/bin/date -Is >> /tmp/workshop-cron.log`. Confirm with `crontab -l`, wait for a matching minute, and remove only your practice line when finished. Absolute paths help when a scheduler has a smaller environment than your interactive shell.

For a systemd alternative, create `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-log.service` with the first block and `/etc/systemd/system/workshop-log.timer` with the second. The shared base name associates the timer with the service.

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Write workshop journal entry
[Service]
Type=oneshot
ExecStart=/usr/bin/logger -t workshop-timer tick
```

```ini
[Unit]
Description=Run workshop log job
[Timer]
OnCalendar=*-*-* *:*:00
AccuracySec=1s
Persistent=true
[Install]
WantedBy=timers.target
```

Reload systemd, `sudo systemctl enable --now workshop-log.timer`, and inspect `systemctl list-timers --all workshop-log.timer`. After a minute read `journalctl -t workshop-timer -b`. Disable your practice timer when finished. For a time client use `timedatectl`, `chronyc sources -v` and `chronyc tracking`. On a guest with a designated reachable NTP source, add one `server YOUR_NTP_SOURCE iburst` directive with the real address to `/etc/chrony.conf`, restart chronyd and check for a selected source (`^*`). The private exam network supplies no time server. Merely starting chronyd does not prove synchronization.

lessons.title: Lab • Restore a startup service
lessons.body:
On the **server**, the supplied `erudior-maint.service` creates a runtime marker. Start it now and enable it for future boots. Inspect the supplied unit before you change its state.

Use two systemctl queries to verify active and enabled independently. Then inspect `/run/erudior-maint.ready` and the unit's journal. If it is active but disabled, decide what the next reboot would do. If it is enabled but failed, read the first error in the current boot. Leave the supplied unit performing its original job and submit for the reboot check.

lessons.title: Trace a request from name to interface to listener
lessons.body:
A user can reach a file server by address but cannot reach it by name. Test the same name lookup the application uses before changing routes. On the client compare `getent ahostsv4 server.workshop.test`, `ip route get 192.168.77.10` and `ip -brief address`. On the server inspect listening TCP sockets with `ss -lnt`. A resolver failure, missing route and closed listener have different remedies.

Add `192.168.77.10 server.workshop.test` once to the client's `/etc/hosts`, then run `getent ahostsv4 server.workshop.test | awk '{print $1}' | sort -u`. Expect one unique address. Multiple rows for stream and datagram socket types are normal. Check `grep '^hosts:' /etc/nsswitch.conf` to see where applications look up hosts. `dig` queries DNS directly and may miss a valid local hosts entry.

## Configure a practice interface without changing the lab link
In the untimed client with NetworkManager available, create a dummy profile. Check that `workshop-dummy` and `dummy42` are unused first.

```sh
sudo nmcli connection add type dummy ifname dummy42 con-name workshop-dummy ipv4.method manual ipv4.addresses 192.0.2.44/24 ipv6.method manual ipv6.addresses 2001:db8:42::44/64
sudo nmcli connection modify workshop-dummy connection.autoconnect yes
sudo nmcli connection up workshop-dummy
ip -brief address show dummy42
nmcli -f connection.autoconnect,ipv4.addresses,ipv6.addresses connection show workshop-dummy
```

Verify both addresses and the autoconnect setting. Reboot the workshop guest and verify again. Remove only the practice profile using `sudo nmcli connection delete workshop-dummy`. Keep the engine-provided interface unchanged. A connection profile persists configuration; commands such as `ip addr add` change runtime state.

lessons.title: Lab • Make the file server discoverable
lessons.body:
On the **client**, make `files.lab.test` consistently resolve to the server at `192.168.77.10` for IPv4 applications, including after startup. Preserve the existing localhost and guest mappings.

Look up the exact name with `getent ahostsv4` and list its distinct addresses. A ping to the numeric IP only tests a different part of the path. If two different addresses appear, inspect the matching hosts entries and the resolver order. Recheck with a fresh command before submitting.

lessons.title: Control who can connect and what they can reach
lessons.body:
Use the untimed pair as an approved client and server. On the server inspect `systemctl status sshd` and `ss -lnt`. If OpenSSH server is installed but inactive, enable it with `sudo systemctl enable --now sshd`. Use your own guest account for this exercise.

On the client generate a dedicated key with `ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -f ~/.ssh/workshop_id` and supply a passphrase. Compare the server's console output from `ssh-keygen -lf /etc/ssh/ssh_host_ed25519_key.pub` with the ED25519 host fingerprint when accepting the first connection. Use a key algorithm supported by the guest's crypto policy. If SSH password login for learner is allowed, copy the public key with `ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id.pub learner@192.168.77.10`. Otherwise log in locally on the server as learner, create `~/.ssh` with mode 700 and append the single line from the client's **.pub** file to `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`. Set that file to 600 and restore its default SELinux context with `restorecon -RFv ~/.ssh`. Only the public key is copied.

Run `ssh -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id -o IdentitiesOnly=yes learner@192.168.77.10 hostname`. Then transfer your own note using `scp -i ~/.ssh/workshop_id notes.txt learner@192.168.77.10:notes.received`. Create `notes.txt` locally first. Compare `sha256sum` on the two files. For a failed login, check the account, file ownership, mode, and `sudo journalctl -b -u sshd` on the server.

## Test a firewall rule in two stores
On a workshop guest with active firewalld, inspect `sudo firewall-cmd --get-active-zones`. Identify the zone for the test interface and substitute its name for ZONE. For an unused demonstration TCP port, query `sudo firewall-cmd --zone=ZONE --query-port=18080/tcp` in runtime and with `--permanent`. If neither allows it, add it first at runtime with `--add-port=18080/tcp` and repeat both queries. Make it persistent with the same add command plus `--permanent`. Reload and verify both queries. Remove only your two practice rules when finished. Opening a firewall port permits traffic to reach a listener; verify listening separately with `ss -lnt`.

lessons.title: Diagnose a denial while keeping access controls intact
lessons.body:
A web document is readable by ordinary file mode, yet a confined service cannot access it. Check identity, traversal and standard permissions, then examine SELinux. Use `getenforce`, `ls -Zd /var/www/html`, `ps -eZ` and `sudo ausearch -m AVC -ts recent` when the audit tools are present. Compare an affected file's type with `matchpathcon /var/www/html/example.txt`. The policy convention for read-only web content under the normal document root is `httpd_sys_content_t`.

In the untimed server, create a practice file under `/var/www/html`, using `sudo mkdir -p /var/www/html` if needed. Predict its type. Inspect it with `ls -Z` and then run `sudo restorecon -v /var/www/html/example.txt` on the file you created. A file moved from another directory can retain its old label. A copy or rename is no substitute for checking the resulting context.

## Move the policy with the application
For an alternate document root on a guest with semanage, create `/srv/workshop-web` and a test file. Add the path rule `sudo semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/workshop-web(/.*)?'`, then apply it with `sudo restorecon -Rv /srv/workshop-web`. Check actual and expected labels. For a web service that needs a different listening port, inspect `semanage port -l` and, on an unused training port with no existing specific assignment, practice `sudo semanage port -a -t http_port_t -p tcp 18081`. Verify the mapping and remove your new mapping when finished. Firewall policy and SELinux port labels are independent.

Inspect `getsebool httpd_can_network_connect` and `semanage boolean -l`. In a disposable guest where that capability is needed, record the current value, apply `sudo setsebool -P httpd_can_network_connect on` and verify, then restore the original value. To observe enforcement modes on the untimed disposable guest only, record the current mode, compare `getenforce` after `sudo setenforce 0` and `sudo setenforce 1`, and finish in enforcing mode. A denial identifies a policy decision to investigate. For ordinary default permissions, compare newly created files and directories under `umask 027` in a subshell. Expect 640 and 750 from ordinary creation modes.

lessons.title: Lab • Repair a web document label
lessons.body:
On the **server**, create the regular file `/var/www/html/erudior-status.txt` and give it the SELinux type for ordinary read-only web content, `httpd_sys_content_t`. Leave enforcement enabled. A short status line of your choice is sufficient.

Inspect the actual file type and context, the expected default context for this path, and the global enforcement mode. Avoid following a symlink to an unrelated file. If a relabel changes the type back, inspect the path's persistent policy mapping. Submit after the actual file and mode satisfy the task.

lessons.title: Rehearsal • Hand off a working file service
lessons.body:
A shift change is approaching. The client needs an operator and a way to find and consume the server's data. The server needs a private team workspace and a dependable startup service. Use the five task cards below as the acceptance criteria. This timed rehearsal starts with fresh machines. It does not inherit work from the individual labs.

Before opening a console, draw two columns headed Client and Server. Allocate 5 minutes to map the tasks, 30 to implement them and 15 to test as the affected user. Verify the lookup and mount from the client. Verify ownership and startup behavior on the server. Partition your checks so a failure in one area does not mask evidence in another. For example, test address routing independently of hostname lookup.

Each task is worth 10 points. After submission identify the first missing observation and return to the corresponding lab. Aim to earn all 50 points before moving on.

lessons.title: Rehearsal • Bring a branch server back into service
lessons.body:
A branch office is returning to service. Its client needs a usable software source and a command an ordinary operator can execute. Its server needs memory backing, a tuning policy and a document with the correct security label. Work from the five task cards below. Use a fresh evidence sheet and solve them without consulting the earlier command examples.

Reserve the last 10 minutes for verification. Record the repository ID, two classifier boundary results, the active profile, usable swap and the file context. If a persistent setting looks right on disk, identify the live query that establishes it has actually taken effect. Submit once you have tested the operator's experience. Each task is worth 10 points.

Review both columns of the result. If everything passed before reboot but one item failed afterward, name the component responsible for restoring that item at boot. Repeat the corresponding focused lab before the final practical.

lessons.title: Final • RHCSA practice exam for RHEL 10
lessons.body:
You have a new client, a new server and three hours. Read the ten tasks in the exam panel. Use the named machine for each and decide your own order. Both machines should identify as RHEL 10 or compatible Enterprise Linux 10 during preparation.

Choose **Prepare machines**. When ready, choose **Begin**. You may use the documentation installed in the guests. For an independent rehearsal, put course notes aside until you submit. Keep a short record of which task works now and what will make it work at boot. Reserve time to test from the client's or service user's point of view.

**Submit exam** closes the consoles. The grader checks the requested state at submission, restarts the relevant machines and checks again. A task earns its 30 points when both checks pass. The ten tasks total 300 practice points, with an Erudior target of 210. Results appear in this lesson and in course **Progress**. The numerical VM result records practical performance. A lesson completion checkmark records study progress. Use **Review task checks** and the next lesson to plan a retake.

Erudior authored this fixed practice form using the published EX200 objectives. Its tasks, weights and passing target are Erudior's own. A repeat uses the same form, so use the transfer exercises in the next lesson to judge whether you can apply the skill to a new request.

lessons.title: Read your result and plan a targeted retake
lessons.body:
Open **Progress**, then return to the final exam lesson and expand **Review task checks**. Pick one task. Record the target machine, the requested end state, what you observed at submission and what the grader observed after reboot. For any lost points, identify a specific change and one command that would expose its absence.

| Report area | Revisit this lab | Independent transfer exercise in the untimed pair |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Essential tools | Hand off a team workspace | Make a second group's directory and verify the group of a newly created child. |
| Users and groups | Add a client operator | Add a second group without removing the first and test through a fresh login. |
| Software management | Bring an offline RPM source online | Give the supplied shelf a new repository ID and refresh metadata with only that ID enabled. |
| Shell scripts | Deliver an executable classifier | Use a threshold of 25 and demonstrate both boundary cases as an ordinary user. |
| Running systems | Apply a persistent performance profile | Select a different installed profile and confirm it after startup. |
| Local storage | Add persistent swap capacity | Activate a different-sized swap file and compare its requested and usable sizes. |
| File systems | Recover a share on demand | Mount the same export on demand at a different client path and prove its source. |
| Deployment and maintenance | Restore a startup service | Write your own oneshot that creates a different marker in /run on each boot. |
| Basic networking | Make the file server discoverable | Add a new alias, then distinguish an address lookup from a reachability test. |
| Security | Repair a web document label | Use a second document path and verify expected and actual types after restorecon. |

**Failed at submission:** reproduce the symptom in the affected account and guest. Check prerequisites, names, paths and active state before persistence. **Passed at submission, failed after reboot:** inspect startup enablement, persistent configuration and the new boot's journal. **Both checks passed:** attempt the transfer exercise with new names or values and explain why it still works. If grading was interrupted, reopen the lesson and use **Retry grading** where offered. A technical interruption and an observed incorrect configuration need different follow-up.

A retake uses **Reset exam disks** in the final lesson. Copy any notes or scores you want to compare first. Starting over removes that attempt's guest changes. Practice until you can verify a fresh configuration unaided, including the independent exercises outside the ten machine-graded tasks.

## Keep the official scope handy
Review the published objective list alongside your results. The RHEL manuals give the command syntax and platform conventions used throughout the course.

- [Red Hat EX200 objectives and exam format](https://www.redhat.com/en/services/training/ex200-red-hat-certified-system-administrator-rhcsa-exam)
- [Red Hat Enterprise Linux 10 documentation](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10)
- [Managing storage devices](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html-single/managing_storage_devices/index)
- [Configuring and managing networking](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html-single/configuring_and_managing_networking/index)
- [Administering RHEL with GNOME, including Flatpak](https://docs.redhat.com/en/documentation/red_hat_enterprise_linux/10/html-single/administering_rhel_by_using_the_gnome_desktop_environment/index)

banks.title: RHEL 10 administration • Knowledge checks
banks.description: Written checks supporting the lessons. Open the final practical lesson to take the scored two-VM exam.

questions.stem: Two consoles look identical. What most reliably tells you which guest you are about to change?
choices: Compare the shell prompt characters on both machines.
Check its hostname and interface address.
Compare the default login account names.
questions.explanation: The prompt and tools can match on both machines. The seeded server uses .10 and the client uses .20.

questions.stem: When does the timed practical start counting down?
choices: When you import the course.
When you first open a console in the untimed lab.
When you select Begin after guest preparation.
questions.explanation: Preparation and first boot precede the timer. Leaving a running timed lesson does not pause its deadline.

questions.stem: You rename a log on the same filesystem. Which name can still read the original data without any repair?
choices: A second hard link to the same inode.
A symbolic link targeting the old pathname.
A symbolic link in the parent directory targeting the old pathname.
questions.explanation: A hard link is another name for the inode. A symbolic link follows the path stored in the link.

questions.stem: New files in a project directory must inherit its group. What setting belongs on the directory?
choices: The sticky bit alone.
Setgid and appropriate group access.
Group write permission alone.
questions.explanation: Setgid controls group inheritance. The ordinary group mode controls reading, creation and traversal.

questions.stem: An existing operator needs one more group and must retain two current groups. Which command does that?
choices: usermod -G dispatch fieldops
usermod -g dispatch fieldops
usermod -aG dispatch fieldops
questions.explanation: Append preserves other supplementary memberships. A fresh login loads the updated group list.

questions.stem: Which evidence shows both the maximum password age and warning period for a local account?
choices: chage -l with the account name
getent group with the account name
passwd -S without the target account name
questions.explanation: chage reads account-aging fields. Membership and home directory permissions do not encode them.

questions.stem: The file is /media/content/repodata/repomd.xml. Which local repository URL points to its root?
choices: file:///media/content/repodata/repomd.xml
file:///media/content
file:///media
questions.explanation: DNF builds the metadata path beneath baseurl. The root contains the repodata directory.

questions.stem: A learner installed a Flatpak with --user. Where should they first look for the installed app?
choices: rpm -qa
dnf repolist --enabled
flatpak list --user --app
questions.explanation: A per-user Flatpak belongs to that account’s Flatpak installation. RPM inventory and DNF source listings describe different objects.

questions.stem: A script has two filename arguments, one containing a space. How should its loop expand the positional parameters?
choices: Use a double-quoted expansion of the at-sign parameter.
Use a double-quoted expansion of the asterisk parameter.
Expand only the first positional argument.
questions.explanation: Quoted "$@" preserves argument boundaries for a loop. Quoted "$*" joins the arguments, and $1 covers only the first.

questions.stem: A classifier changes category at 5. Which pair best detects a misplaced less-than-or-equal comparison?
choices: 0 and 1
4 and 5
12 and 13
questions.explanation: Adjacent inputs on opposite sides of the threshold reveal whether the threshold itself is in the intended category.

questions.stem: A background process moves from nice 5 to nice 10. What usually happens when CPU time is contested?
choices: It takes priority over normal processes with smaller nice values.
It is capped at ten percent of a CPU.
Other normal-priority processes get preference over it.
questions.explanation: Increasing the nice value lowers its scheduling priority. It remains eligible to run.

questions.stem: A failure happened before the last reboot. Which first query narrows the investigation to the affected boot and service?
choices: journalctl -b -1 -u NAME
journalctl -b -u NAME
systemctl list-unit-files
questions.explanation: The -1 boot offset selects the previous boot. That boot must have been retained by the journal.

questions.stem: How can you use rescue.target for one boot while keeping the configured startup default?
choices: Set rescue.target as the default indefinitely.
Select it with a one-time kernel command-line argument in GRUB.
Remove multi-user.target as a dependency from a single service.
questions.explanation: GRUB entry edits at the boot menu apply to that invocation. systemctl set-default changes normal future boots.

questions.stem: An LV grew by 128 MiB, but df shows the old XFS size. What should you check next?
choices: Whether df needs the UUID in /etc/fstab to display the new size.
Whether unmounting alone will make XFS grow to the new size.
Whether the mounted XFS filesystem was grown as well.
questions.explanation: Device capacity and filesystem capacity are tracked separately. Inspect lvs and df, then grow the mounted XFS filesystem when needed.

questions.stem: Which order follows storage from backing device to usable LVM space?
choices: Physical volume, volume group, logical volume, filesystem.
Filesystem, volume group, partition, logical volume.
Logical volume, partition, physical volume, volume group.
questions.explanation: A VG pools physical volumes. An LV allocates extents from that pool and can hold a filesystem.

questions.stem: Which observation after a reboot demonstrates that a swap file is in use by the kernel?
choices: The file exists with mode 600.
Its path appears in swapon --show.
Its path appears once in /etc/fstab.
questions.explanation: Mode and configuration support activation. swapon --show reports the active swap areas.

questions.stem: Why use the filesystem UUID in a persistent mount entry?
choices: It makes a mount succeed even when its backing disk is missing.
It makes a mount independent of its filesystem driver.
It identifies the filesystem even if the device name changes.
questions.explanation: A filesystem UUID is independent of disk discovery order. Check the identifier and filesystem type before rebooting.

questions.stem: The autofs service is active. What is the best next test of the end-user outcome?
choices: Open the remote marker through its client path, then inspect the mounted source and type.
List the local mountpoint without opening its contents.
Count entries in /etc/exports on the client.
questions.explanation: Reading the file triggers the mount. Checking the filesystem serving it distinguishes remote content from a local look-alike.

questions.stem: A new oneshot unit has been started but never enabled. It is active now. What has been established?
choices: It is guaranteed to start after reboot.
It ran this boot; its automatic activation still needs separate verification.
Its process must keep running indefinitely.
questions.explanation: Active and enabled describe different things. A oneshot can remain active after its program exits.

questions.stem: Why use a marker in /run to verify a service after reboot?
choices: Files there are permanently archived across boots.
All changes to /run are automatically written to the unit definition.
A new boot recreates /run, so something in this boot had to recreate the marker.
questions.explanation: A marker created in volatile runtime storage provides stronger evidence of a fresh service invocation than a file left on a persistent filesystem.

questions.stem: chronyd is active. Which observation best supports a claim that it is synchronizing with a particular source?
choices: chronyc sources -v shows that source as selected.
The chronyd unit file exists.
The designated source appears in /etc/chrony.conf.
questions.explanation: A selected source and tracking data show synchronization. An enabled daemon or configured time zone cannot establish that a source was reachable.

questions.stem: The local hosts file supplies the name. Which check resembles a normal IPv4 application lookup?
choices: dig followed by a public resolver address
getent ahostsv4 followed by the hostname
ss -lnt on the server
questions.explanation: getent uses the guest name service configuration, including local files when configured. DNS-only queries can give a different answer.

questions.stem: An address added with ip is lost at reboot. Where should you record both IPv4 and IPv6 configuration on a NetworkManager guest?
choices: As a second ip address add command on the live interface.
In an ifup command typed at the current shell.
In the intended NetworkManager connection profile, with autoconnect verified.
questions.explanation: Profiles define persistent network configuration. Shell history and logs cannot reactivate addresses.

questions.stem: Which item should be installed on the target account for public-key SSH authentication?
choices: The client’s public key in that account’s authorized_keys.
The server’s public host key in the client account’s authorized_keys.
The client’s public key only in the client account’s known_hosts.
questions.explanation: The server checks proof that the client holds the matching private key. Only the public half belongs in authorized_keys.

questions.stem: After a firewalld reload a test opening vanished. What paired checks would have exposed this beforehand?
choices: Compare the runtime port listing twice in the default zone.
Query that port in the interface zone in both runtime and permanent configuration.
Query only the permanent rules for a different network zone.
questions.explanation: Reload replaces runtime state with permanent policy. Both stores and the zone must match the intended outcome.

questions.stem: Which pair makes a new custom web root recover its intended labels after restorecon?
choices: Change only the current file context with chcon.
Set the web service port type without updating the file mapping.
Define a persistent fcontext mapping, then apply it with restorecon.
questions.explanation: The mapping supplies the policy expectation for future relabels. restorecon applies that expected context to the existing tree.

questions.stem: A process requests mode 0666 with umask 027 and no default ACL. What is the resulting regular-file mode?
questions.explanation: The mask removes group write and all permissions for others. Regular-file creation did not request any execute bits.

questions.stem: A server task passed before reboot and failed afterward. What should your first retake investigation compare?
choices: Only the output captured before the first reboot.
Its startup configuration and new-boot journal against its observed live state.
Whether another guest currently has the right live configuration.
questions.explanation: The earlier check established a working live state. Startup configuration and logs can explain why the guest did not recreate it.
